summary: Raises the susceptibility of the ARPANET to security violations. Its title echoes the opening of a well-known Christmas poem.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 602 warns that ARPANET systems could be misused because of weak passwords and anonymous access through TIPs. It cites recent incidents and urges the network community to take the risk seriously.

questions: what security risks did rfc 602 identify
why were arpanet tips a security concern
subtitle: A warning about weak passwords, unauthenticated TIP access and break-ins.

tldr.problem: The author says ARPANET systems were vulnerable because of guessable passwords, TIP access without user identification and people seeking to break into systems.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC describes these risks and reports recent incidents: two major serving hosts had crashed under suspicious circumstances, and a system wheel password had been compromised.
tldr.outcome: The note warns that security violations may be more numerous than known and urges readers not to wait passively for the problem to resolve.

today: RFC 602 is a 1973 warning about security weaknesses and incidents on the ARPANET.

sections.title: Three Sources of Security Risk
sections.content: The RFC identifies three reasons for security violations. Some sites had not adapted to remote access and still used easy-to-guess passwords, such as first names, initials, reversed host names or keyboard sequences. TIP phone numbers were publicly posted, and a TIP did not require user identification before providing network access. The author also describes a continuing interest among some people in breaking into systems.
sections.plainLanguage: Some passwords were easy to guess, and a person could reach a TIP without first identifying themselves. The author also says some people treated breaking into systems as a challenge.

sections.title: Incidents the Author Cites
sections.content: The author says the situation would be humorous if recent events were not serious: at least two major serving hosts had crashed under suspicious circumstances in recent weeks, and a system wheel password had been compromised by two high school students in Los Angeles. The RFC does not give names for these systems or further details about the incidents.
sections.plainLanguage: The author points to recent incidents as evidence that the risks were real. The note does not identify the affected hosts.

sections.title: A Call to Take the Risk Seriously
sections.content: The author suspects that dangerous security violations are increasing and may be more common than the community knows. The RFC ends by warning readers not to wait passively for a solution.
sections.plainLanguage: The author urges people responsible for network systems to act rather than assume that someone else will solve the security problem.
